topic: Learn LLM Inference Engineering: From KV Cache to PagedAttention

key_points: Attention is O(n²) without KV cache; the cache converts each decode step from quadratic to linear in sequence length
KV cache stores K,V tensors from previous tokens so they don't need recomputation; each decode step only computes K,V for the new token
KV cache memory formula: 2 × num_layers × num_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element per token; a 70B-class model at 128k context with batch 8 can reach ~335 GB, exceeding model weights
FlashAttention tiles attention into SRAM blocks, cutting HBM reads by ~10x; now near-universal
GQA shares K,V pairs across groups of query heads, cutting KV cache by up to 8x (e.g. 8 KV heads instead of 64)
PagedAttention treats KV cache as paged virtual memory (fixed-size pages + block table) to eliminate fragmentation under concurrent load

LLM inference splits into two phases: Prefill (process prompt tokens in parallel, creates K/V state, latency signal = TTFT) and Decode (one token per step, reads historical K/V, latency signal = TPOT)
Without caching, generating the 100th token requires re-processing the first 99 tokens — computational redundancy
KV cache stores historical Key and Value tensors, eliminating repeated projection; attention still scans the cached sequence each step
Trade-off: lower compute for higher memory capacity and bandwidth demand
Covers KV cache memory calculation in practice and advanced optimization techniques
PagedAttention (Kwon et al., UC Berkeley 2023) applies OS virtual memory to KV cache: virtual KV slot → block table → physical block
GPU memory split into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens each); blocks allocated on-demand as sequence grows; internal fragmentation < 1 block
Blocks can be SHARED across requests with the same prefix
Covers the full serving stack: prefix caching, continuous batching, quantization (INT8/NF4/GPTQ/AWQ), speculative decoding, tensor/pipeline parallelism
Compares vLLM vs TGI vs TensorRT-LLM frameworks
Inference speed is a memory problem before it is a compute problem
A 70B-parameter model spends most time re-reading what it already wrote — every new token attends to every previous token
LLM inference pipeline = managing memory, scheduling requests, optimizing the token-by-token generation loop
Covers the arithmetic that determines latency budget: inference latency vs throughput vs time-to-first-token
Assumes familiarity with quantization, vLLM, paged attention, speculative decoding, SGLang
Above 128K context, KV cache memory is bigger than parameter memory; at 1M tokens it's 60-85% of wall-clock and 70-90% of GPU memory
Five optimization families collapse KV cost by 4-40x: paged attention, prefix caching, MQA/GQA/MLA, KV-cache quantization
Paged attention is the substrate (required, not optional) — without it you waste 30-50% of VRAM under variable-length batches
Prefix caching gives 85-95% cost savings on cache hits; hit-rates of 60-85% achievable on agent loops/multi-tenant SaaS
DeepSeek MLA compresses KV cache 7-14x via low-rank projection; GQA gives 4-8x; FP8 KV cache halves memory with sub-1% accuracy regression
Stacking optimizations compounds: MLA + FP8 drops KV from 135 GB to 8 GB at 1M context (17x reduction)

stats.fact: Attention complexity is O(n²) with sequence length; doubling context quadruples attention compute. The KV cache converts each decode step from quadratic to linear (O(n)).
KV cache memory per token = 2 × num_layers × num_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element. A 70B-class model (80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128-dim, FP16) uses ~0.32 MB per token.
At 128k context, a single request's KV cache on a large 70B-class model can consume tens of gigabytes — comparable to or exceeding the model weights at INT4.
GQA with 8 KV heads instead of 64 reduces KV cache memory by 8x, making long-context inference viable without quality loss.
FlashAttention's original paper reported an order-of-magnitude reduction in HBM memory reads by tiling attention into SRAM blocks.
PagedAttention (Kwon et al., UC Berkeley 2023) splits GPU memory into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens each), allocated on-demand, with internal fragmentation < 1 block.
Without paged attention, GPU memory fragments rapidly under variable-length batches, wasting 30-50% of available VRAM; effective utilization drops to 50-65% under bursty traffic.
Above 128K context, KV cache memory exceeds parameter memory. On Llama 70B at 1M context, KV cache hits ~135 GB at FP16 — more than the 140 GB of FP16 model weights.
Prefix caching gives 85-95% cost savings on cache hits; hit-rates of 60-85% are achievable on agent loops, multi-tenant SaaS, repo Q&A, and long-doc workflows, dropping per-call cost by 5-12x.

DeepSeek's Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses KV cache 7-14x by storing a low-rank projection; GQA gives 4-8x compression. MLA + FP8 drops KV from 135 GB to 8 GB at 1M context (17x reduction).

FP8 KV cache halves memory with 0.3-0.7 point accuracy regression (within noise); INT8 costs 1.5-3 points on long-context retrieval. The 50% memory savings translate to 30-50% throughput gains via larger batch size.
LLM inference splits into Prefill (parallel prompt processing, latency = TTFT) and Decode (one token per step, latency = TPOT, memory-bandwidth-bound).

angles: Frame inference as a memory problem before a compute problem — the KV cache is the hidden cost line on every long-context deployment
Walk the reader from first principles (attention, O(n²)) to production serving (PagedAttention, vLLM) as a single coherent learning path
Use the OS virtual-memory analogy to make PagedAttention intuitive: virtual KV slot → block table → physical block
Quantify the compounding effect of stacking optimizations (GQA/MLA + FP8 + prefix caching) rather than treating them in isolation
Give a practical decision guide: which technique to apply by workload (long-doc, agent loops, multi-tenant SaaS, high-throughput)
Explain the prefill vs decode split as the mental model that unlocks all inference optimization
Compare serving frameworks (vLLM vs SGLang vs TensorRT-LLM) and when each wins
